tagline: A letter from Paul to his coworker Timothy in Ephesus on false teaching, worship, church leadership, and the life of God's household.
overview:
First Timothy is a letter of instruction to a younger leader left in charge of a troubled church. Paul has gone on to Macedonia and has asked Timothy to stay in Ephesus, where certain teachers were spreading speculation about myths, genealogies, and the law, forbidding marriage and certain foods, and treating godliness as a way to get rich. The letter tells Timothy how to confront them and, just as important, how the church should live: how it should pray, who may lead it and what kind of people they must be, how it should care for widows and honor its elders, and how rich and poor, slave and free, should conduct themselves.

The letter is practical, but it is not merely administrative. Its practical counsel is threaded with some of the New Testament's most compact confessions of faith: that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1:15), that there is one God and one mediator between God and men (2:5), and the hymn-like summary of Christ's work in 3:16. Paul's goal, he says at the start, is love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith (1:5). Sound teaching matters because it produces that kind of life, and false teaching matters because it destroys it.

First Timothy belongs with 2 Timothy and Titus to a group called the Pastoral Letters, a name used since the eighteenth century because the three are addressed to individuals charged with pastoral oversight. They have shaped the church's thinking about ministry more than almost any other part of the New Testament, and several of their passages, especially 2:8-15 on women and 3:1-13 on overseers and deacons, remain among the most debated in Scripture.
author:
The letter opens with Paul's name (1:1) and contains personal detail about his past as a persecutor (1:12-16) and his travels (1:3). The church received it as Paul's from early on. Polycarp of Smyrna, writing in the first half of the second century, appears to echo it; Irenaeus, around AD 180, quotes it and names Paul as its author; and it is included in the Muratorian list of accepted books, usually dated to the late second century. The second-century teacher Marcion did not include the Pastoral Letters in his collection of Paul's letters, and the early papyrus P46 (around AD 200) does not contain them, though its final pages are missing, so it is uncertain whether they were ever there.

Since the early nineteenth century many scholars have concluded that a later follower of Paul wrote the Pastoral Letters in his name. They point to vocabulary and style that differ from Paul's undisputed letters (words such as godliness and sound teaching are frequent here and rare elsewhere), to a more settled church order with overseers, deacons, and enrolled widows, to a false teaching that some see as closer to second-century movements, and to the difficulty of fitting the letters' travel notes into the story of Acts. On this view the letters are a faithful attempt to apply Paul's legacy to a later generation, following a practice of writing in a revered teacher's name that was known in the ancient world.

Scholars who hold that Paul wrote them answer that differences in vocabulary reflect different subjects and a different kind of letter (written to trusted coworkers rather than to congregations), that the church order described is simple and shows no single bishop over the elders, that the false teaching fits a first-century mix of Jewish speculation and ascetic practice, and that the travels fit a period after Acts ends, if Paul was released from his first Roman imprisonment, as early tradition reports. They also note that the early church rejected letters it knew to be written under a false name. Mediating views hold that Paul used a secretary who was given freedom in wording (some have suggested Luke, who is named as Paul's companion in 2 Timothy 4:11), or, as P. N. Harrison argued in 1921, that genuine fragments of Paul's notes were worked into letters completed later. Evangelical scholarship largely holds to Paul's authorship; a majority of critical scholars do not.
date: If Paul wrote the letter, it most likely comes from the period after his release from house arrest in Rome (Acts 28:30-31), around AD 62 to 64, when he had left Ephesus for Macedonia (1:3). This requires a release and a further period of travel not recorded in Acts; Clement of Rome (around AD 96) says Paul reached the limit of the west, and the fourth-century historian Eusebius reports a release and a second imprisonment. A minority of scholars who accept Paul's authorship try to fit the letter within the Acts period, for example during Paul's years in Ephesus (Acts 19) or soon after, though the details fit awkwardly. Scholars who see the letter as written by a later follower usually date it between about AD 80 and 110, and some later still.
setting:
Ephesus was one of the great cities of the Roman Empire, a port on the west coast of Asia Minor (modern Turkey) and the leading city of the province of Asia. It was famous for its temple of Artemis, one of the wonders of the ancient world, and for magic and religious practice of many kinds. Paul had spent about three years there (Acts 19; 20:31), and a large church had grown up, meeting in households across the city. When he said farewell to its elders, Paul warned that men would arise from among them speaking twisted things to draw disciples after them (Acts 20:29-30). This letter shows that warning coming true.

Timothy came from Lystra in Asia Minor, the son of a Jewish mother who believed and a Greek father (Acts 16:1). He had traveled with Paul since the second missionary trip, had been sent on several delicate errands (1 Corinthians 4:17; 1 Thessalonians 3:2), and is named as co-sender of six of Paul's letters. He was younger than many in the church (4:12) and seems to have been in poor health (5:23). His task in Ephesus was not to found a church but to correct one.
purpose: Paul writes so that Timothy, and the church through him, will know how people ought to conduct themselves in God's household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth (3:15). The letter equips Timothy to silence false teachers, to restore order to the church's worship, to see that leaders are chosen for their character, to organize care for widows, to deal fairly with elders who sin, and to warn the rich. It is also personal encouragement to a younger leader: keep your conscience clear, watch your life and your teaching, and do not let anyone despise your youth.
story: Acts tells the story of how the good news spread from Jerusalem to Rome, and Paul's letters to churches show it taking root in cities across the empire. The Pastoral Letters show the next step: the apostolic generation passing responsibility to those who will carry the faith after them. First Timothy stands at that handover. It looks back to the gospel Paul received and forward to a church that must guard the deposit of faith without an apostle on hand. After it comes 2 Timothy, Paul's last letter, written as he faces death, and Titus, a close companion to 1 Timothy addressed to churches on Crete.
christ: At the center of the letter's concern for order stands a person. Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and Paul counts himself the worst of them (1:15). There is one mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all (2:5-6). The hymn of 3:16 traces his story from his appearing in the flesh to his being taken up in glory, and the letter's closing charge points to his confession before Pontius Pilate and to his coming appearance (6:13-14). Sound teaching, in this letter, is the teaching that agrees with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ (6:3); the church's order exists to guard and display the truth about him.
reading: First Timothy is a real letter written to a real person in a particular crisis. Read it as the practical application of the gospel to a specific church, and ask at each point what problem in Ephesus Paul is addressing. The letter is not a complete church manual, and its instructions on widows or slaves assume social institutions very different from ours. Watch for the repeated trustworthy sayings (1:15; 3:1; 4:9), which seem to quote early Christian teaching, and for the contrast between sound, healthy teaching and the diseased speculation of the opponents. Where the letter is contested (on women, on church offices, on authorship), read the arguments of more than one side before settling, and notice that Christians who share the same confession about Christ reach different conclusions.

structure.title: The charge against false teaching
structure.summary: Paul urges Timothy to stay in Ephesus and stop the false teachers, sets the law in its proper place, and recalls the mercy shown to him, the worst of sinners.

structure.title: Order in God's household
structure.summary: Instructions on prayer for all people, on men and women in worship, and on the character required of overseers and deacons, closing with a confession of the mystery of godliness.

structure.title: False asceticism and a faithful minister
structure.summary: Paul exposes teaching that forbids marriage and foods and urges Timothy to train himself for godliness and give himself to Scripture, teaching, and example.

structure.title: Caring for the whole family
structure.summary: How to treat older and younger members, support true widows, honor and discipline elders, and teach slaves.

structure.title: Godliness, money, and the final charge
structure.summary: False teachers treat religion as a way to profit; Paul warns against the love of money, charges Timothy to fight the good fight, and instructs the rich to be generous.

themes.title: Sound teaching and a good conscience
themes.body: The letter speaks of sound, literally healthy, teaching, and sets it against speculation that breeds quarrels. Teaching and life are never separated: false teachers have shipwrecked their faith by rejecting a good conscience (1:19), and Timothy will save himself and his hearers by watching both his life and his doctrine (4:16). Truth, in this letter, is meant to make people well.

themes.title: The church as God's household
themes.body: Paul calls the church God's household (3:15), and the image shapes the whole letter. Leaders must manage their own households well, members are to treat one another as fathers, mothers, brothers, and sisters (5:1-2), and families are to care for their own widows. The church is not a lecture hall or a club but a family under God, with the order and mutual obligations a household requires.

themes.title: Godliness
themes.body: The word translated godliness (eusebeia) appears more often in the Pastoral Letters than anywhere else in the New Testament. It names reverence for God worked out in everyday conduct. The false teachers treat it as a means of gain; Paul answers that godliness with contentment is great gain (6:6) and urges Timothy to train for it as an athlete trains (4:7-8).

themes.title: God the Savior of all people
themes.body: The letter repeatedly calls God Savior and stresses the universal reach of his saving will: he wants everyone to be saved (2:4), Christ gave himself as a ransom for all (2:6), and God is the Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe (4:10). These verses stand behind the church's prayer for all people, including rulers, and its mission to the nations.

themes.title: Wealth and contentment
themes.body: Money runs through the letter: leaders must be free of the love of money, false teachers seek profit, and the letter's closing section warns that the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil (6:10). Yet Paul does not condemn the rich; he charges them to be rich in good works and to hope in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy (6:17).

keyChapters.why: Paul's testimony of mercy to the worst of sinners gives the letter its gospel foundation and sets the tone for how Timothy must oppose false teaching.
Contains the confession of one God and one mediator, and the debated instructions on women in worship.
Sets out the character required of overseers and deacons and names the church the pillar and foundation of the truth, closing with an early Christian hymn.
Defends the goodness of creation against false asceticism and gives Timothy a portrait of faithful ministry.
The New Testament's fullest warning about the love of money, and a charge to fight the good fight of the faith.

parts.body:
1 Timothy is a letter from Paul to Timothy, his younger friend and fellow worker, whom he had left in charge of the church in Ephesus. It has 6 chapters and can be read aloud in about twenty minutes.

The church in Ephesus was in trouble. Some of its own teachers had gone wrong. They spun long speculations out of myths and family trees, wanted to be teachers of the law without understanding it, forbade marriage and certain foods, and treated religion as a way to make money. Paul writes to tell Timothy how to stop them, and, just as much, how the church should live: how it should pray, who should lead it and what kind of people they must be, how it should care for widows and honour its elders, and how rich and poor, slave and free, should behave.

Paul says what the letter is for: “so that you will know how each one must conduct himself in God’s household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (3:15). And he says what all teaching is for: “The goal of our instruction is the love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith” (1:5).

The letter is practical, but its practical words are wrapped around some of the shortest and clearest confessions of faith in the Bible. “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst” (1:15). “For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (2:5).

Some passages in this letter are among the most debated in all of Scripture, especially what it says about women (2:8-15) and about church leaders (3:1-13). These notes set out the main readings fairly and take no side where faithful churches differ.

parts.h: Who wrote it: the Pastoral Letters
parts.body:
1 Timothy, 2 Timothy and Titus are often called the Pastoral Letters, a name used since the 1700s, because they are written to men caring for churches. All three open with Paul's name, and 1 Timothy is full of personal detail: Paul's past as a persecutor (1:12-16), his travels (1:3), his hopes to come soon (3:14).

The church received them as Paul's from early on. Irenaeus, around AD 180, quotes 1 Timothy and names Paul as its writer, and it is in the list of accepted books known as the Muratorian list, usually dated to the late second century. But Marcion, a second-century teacher whose views the church rejected, did not include the Pastoral Letters in his collection of Paul's letters, and the oldest surviving copy of Paul's letters, a papyrus from around AD 200, does not have them, though its last pages are lost.

Since the early 1800s many scholars have concluded that a later follower of Paul wrote these letters in his name. Here are their reasons, as they would put them. The words and style differ from the letters nearly everyone accepts as Paul's: words like ‘godliness’ and ‘sound teaching’ are common here and rare elsewhere. The church seems more settled, with overseers, deacons and an enrolled list of widows. The false teaching looks to some like movements of the second century. And Paul's travels in these letters are hard to fit into the story of Acts. On this view, the letters are a faithful attempt to apply Paul's teaching to a later generation, in a world where writing in a revered teacher's name was a known practice.

Many other scholars hold that Paul wrote them. Here are their reasons, as they would put them. Different words fit a different subject and a different kind of letter, written to trusted fellow workers rather than to whole churches. The church order is simple, with no single bishop over the elders. The false teaching fits the first century, a mix of Jewish speculation and strict rules about the body. The travels fit a time after Acts ends, if Paul was released from his first imprisonment in Rome, as early writers report. And the early church rejected letters it knew were written under a false name. Some take a middle way: that Paul gave a trusted secretary freedom with the wording.

These notes do not choose. Both views are held by careful scholars, and readers on both sides take the letters as Scripture. The church received them as Paul's and has read them as Scripture from the beginning. These notes speak of the writer as Paul, as the letters do.

Ephesus was one of the great cities of the Roman world, a port on the west coast of what is now Turkey and the leading city of the province of Asia. Its temple of the goddess Artemis was counted among the wonders of the ancient world, and the city was known for magic and religion of every kind.

Paul had spent about three years there (Acts 19; 20:31), and a large church had grown up, meeting in homes across the city. When he said goodbye to its elders, he warned them: “Even from your own number, men will rise up and distort the truth to draw away disciples after them” (Acts 20:30). This letter shows that warning coming true.

Timothy came from Lystra, in what is now central Turkey. His mother was a Jewish believer and his father a Greek (Acts 16:1). He had travelled with Paul for years, been sent on hard errands (1 Corinthians 4:17; 1 Thessalonians 3:2), and is named beside Paul at the start of six of his letters. Paul calls him “my true child in the faith” (1:2).

He was younger than many in the church: “Let no one despise your youth” (4:12). He seems to have had poor health (5:23). And his task was hard. He was not starting a church. He was correcting one, and some of the people he had to correct were its own teachers.

Paul says he had left Ephesus for Macedonia, in northern Greece, and asked Timothy to stay (1:3). Acts does not tell of this trip.

If Paul wrote the letter, it most likely comes from a time after Acts ends. Acts closes with Paul under guard in Rome for two years (Acts 28:30-31). Early Christian writers report that he was released and travelled again before a second imprisonment and his death: Clement of Rome, around AD 96, says Paul reached ‘the limit of the west’, and the historian Eusebius, in the 300s, tells of a release and a second imprisonment. On this view 1 Timothy was written around AD 62 to 64. A few who hold that Paul wrote it try to fit it within the years Acts covers, though the details fit awkwardly.

Scholars who think a later follower wrote it usually date it between about AD 80 and 110.

Either way, the church in Ephesus is a generation old or less, and its trouble comes from inside.

parts.h: The teaching that troubled the church
parts.body:
Paul never sets out the false teaching in full. He only describes it in passing, so it is wise to say only what the letter shows.

The teachers were taken up with “myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculation” (1:4), perhaps long stories spun out of the family lists and figures of the Old Testament. They wanted “to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying” (1:7). They forbade marriage and required people to keep away from certain foods (4:3). They loved arguments and quarrels over words (6:4). They treated godliness “as a means of gain” (6:5). And they claimed a special ‘knowledge’ (6:20).

Scholars have tried to name this teaching. Many see a mix of Jewish speculation with strict rules about the body. Some see an early form of the movements later called Gnostic, which prized secret knowledge; others think that label comes too early. These notes do not give it a name the letter does not give it.

What is plain is how Paul answers it. He does not answer speculation with more speculation. He answers with the gospel, with the goodness of God's creation (4:4), and with a life of love, a clean conscience and sincere faith (1:5). For Paul, teaching is ‘sound’, literally healthy, when it makes people well.

Greeting and the charge (1:1-20). Stay in Ephesus and stop the false teachers. The law is good when used rightly. Paul's own story: the worst of sinners, shown mercy. Fight the good fight.

Prayer and worship (chapter 2). Pray for everyone, including rulers, because God wants everyone to be saved, and there is one mediator, Christ Jesus. How men and women should conduct themselves in worship.

Leaders (3:1-13). What overseers and deacons must be like: character first.

The heart of it (3:14-16). Why Paul writes, and a short song about Christ: “He appeared in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world, was taken up in glory” (3:16).

A good servant (chapter 4). The false teachers forbid marriage and foods, but everything God made is good. Train yourself for godliness. Do not let anyone despise your youth.

God's household (5:1 to 6:2). Treat older people as parents and younger as brothers and sisters. Care for widows in need. Honour elders who lead well, and deal fairly with accusations against them. Slaves and masters.

Godliness and money (6:3-21). False teachers want gain; godliness with contentment is great gain. The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. A last charge to Timothy, and a word to the rich.

parts.h: Women in the church (2:8-15): what all agree, and how Christians differ
parts.body:
Paul writes, “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet. For Adam was formed first, and then Eve” (2:12-13). These are among the most debated words in the New Testament. Christians who share the same faith in Christ read them differently. It is a question that divides faithful churches, not the faith, and these notes do not choose.

Much is agreed. Men and women are equally made in God's image and equally saved by grace. Paul tells women to learn (2:11), when many in his world did not think women needed religious teaching. He tells men to pray ‘without anger or dissension’ (2:8). And nothing in this passage gives anyone leave to belittle, silence or control a woman, or to treat her as less than a sister in Christ.

Complementarian Christians believe that men and women are equal in worth, and that God has given them different callings in the church, with the office of pastor or elder, and teaching the gathered church with that authority, given to qualified men. They note that Paul grounds his words in the order of creation, Adam formed first, not in local custom, so they believe the rule is meant to last. Many read ‘to teach or to exercise authority’ as two normal tasks of an elder.

Egalitarian Christians believe that men and women are equal in worth and that every role in the church, including pastor and teacher, is open to both, as God gifts them. They note that this letter is shaped from start to finish by false teaching in Ephesus that had drawn in some women (5:13-15), and read Paul's words as aimed at that problem. Many read the rare word for ‘exercise authority’ as closer to ‘domineer’, and the mention of Eve's deception as a picture of women being misled by the false teachers.

The chapter note on 1 Timothy 2 sets out both readings more fully, and the note on Acts 18:24-28, where Priscilla teaches Apollos, shows how each side reads that scene.

Verse 15 is a further puzzle: “Women, however, will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith, love, and holiness, with self-control.” Some read it as the birth of the Saviour through a woman; some as a promise of safety in childbirth; some as women living out their salvation in ordinary family life, against teachers who forbade marriage. On every reading it does not mean that a woman is saved by having children. No woman's salvation or worth depends on bearing children. Many faithful people long for children and never have them, or lose them before birth. Childlessness is not a judgment from God, and it does not measure your faith. Your longing is seen.

Chapter 3 says what overseers and deacons must be like. Almost every item is about character, not talent: “above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not dependent on wine, not violent but gentle, peaceable, and free of the love of money” (3:2-3). He must manage his own home well, not be a recent convert, and have a good name with outsiders. Only one item, ‘able to teach’, is a skill. The rest is the kind of person he is.

Churches today are ordered in different ways, and each reads these verses in its own light. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches, and Methodist churches in their own form, are led by bishops who oversee many congregations. Presbyterian and Reformed churches are led by elders who govern together. Baptist, Congregational and many free churches hold that each local congregation, under Christ, chooses its own leaders. These notes do not choose.

Christians also read ‘the husband of but one wife’ in several ways: a man faithful in marriage, a ban on having more than one wife, a ban on remarriage after divorce, or a rule that leaders be married. And in verse 11 ‘the women’ may be the wives of deacons or women who were deacons themselves. Phoebe is called a deacon in Romans 16:1. Churches also differ on whether the office of overseer is open to women, as the part above sets out. These notes do not choose on any of these.

What all can see is that character comes before gifting. A gifted leader who is violent, greedy or harsh does not meet Paul's standard, however well he preaches. And nothing here shields a leader who does harm. Paul says an accusation against an elder needs ‘two or three witnesses’ (5:19), so that leaders are not ruined by gossip. But he also says that those who persist in sin are to be rebuked in front of everyone, and that all of it must be done ‘without bias’, with nothing done ‘out of partiality’ (5:20-21). That verse must never be used to silence a report of abuse, or to keep a crime from the police. Abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities. A church meeting is never a substitute for that.

parts.h: Godliness is not a means of gain
parts.body:
Money runs all through this letter. Leaders must be ‘free of the love of money’ (3:3). The false teachers treated godliness ‘as a means of gain’ (6:5). And near the end Paul writes some of the Bible's most quoted words about money.

“Of course, godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it” (6:6-7). “Those who want to be rich, however, fall into temptation” (6:9). “For the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil” (6:10).

That verse is often misquoted as ‘money is the root of all evil’. Paul does not say money is evil, or that it is the only root of evil. He says the love of money is a root from which every kind of evil can grow. And he aims it at people who wanted to be rich, some of them religious teachers.

Any teaching that treats faith as a way to get rich, that promises health and wealth to those who give or believe enough, takes the very path Paul warns against. That teaching, often called prosperity teaching, is an error, whoever teaches it. The people caught up in it, often poor and hoping, deserve care, not scorn.

Paul does not condemn the rich. He tells them “not to be conceited and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy” (6:17), and “to be generous and ready to share” (6:18). Wealth is a trust, to be held loosely and given freely.

Sound teaching and a good conscience. ‘Sound’ means healthy. True teaching makes people well; false teaching spreads like a disease. And teaching is never apart from life: some ‘shipwrecked their faith’ by throwing away a good conscience (1:19). Paul tells Timothy, “Pay close attention to your life and to your teaching” (4:16).

The church as God's household. The church is ‘God's household’ (3:15). Leaders must care for their own homes well. Members are to treat one another as fathers, mothers, brothers and sisters (5:1-2). Families care for their own. The church is a family under God, not a club.

Godliness. The word means reverence for God lived out in everyday life. It comes more often in these three letters than anywhere else in the New Testament. Paul tells Timothy to train for it as an athlete trains (4:7-8).

God the Saviour of all people. God “wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (2:4). Christ “gave Himself as a ransom for all” (2:6). That is why the church prays for everyone, including rulers.

Mercy for the worst. Paul calls himself the worst of sinners, shown mercy as an example of Christ's patience ‘to those who would believe in Him’ (1:16). No one is beyond it.

Wealth and contentment. Contentment, generosity and hope in God, not in riches.

Paul says “the law is good, if one uses it legitimately” (1:8), and the list of lawbreakers that follows runs in the order of the second half of the Ten Commandments: those who dishonour parents, murderers, the sexually immoral, ‘slave traders’, liars. In the ancient world slave traders often kidnapped people to sell them, and the law said, “Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death” (Exodus 21:16).

‘One God’ (2:5) is Israel's great confession: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Paul adds ‘one mediator’, Christ Jesus.

In 2:13-14 Paul refers to the story of Adam and Eve: “Then the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground” (Genesis 2:7), and Eve's words, “The serpent deceived me” (Genesis 3:13). How he uses the story is part of the debate described above.

‘Every creation of God is good’ (4:4) echoes the first page of the Bible: “And God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31).

The care of widows is everywhere in the law and the Psalms: “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in His holy habitation” (Psalm 68:5). Paul quotes the law about the ox, “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deuteronomy 25:4), for paying those who teach. And the rule of ‘two or three witnesses’ (5:19) is the law's: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15).

And on money Paul sounds like Job and the Teacher: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I will return” (Job 1:21).

It is not a licence to silence the harmed. Its words on discipline (1:20) and on accusations against elders (5:19) protect the innocent and correct the wrongdoer. They must never be used to protect someone who has done harm, to silence someone who has been harmed, or to keep a crime from the police.

It is not a promise of wealth. It warns that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil, and it names those who treat godliness as gain.

It is not a defence of slavery. Paul writes to slaves in a world he could not change, and he names slave traders among the lawbreakers (1:10). The notes on chapter 6 say more.

It is not a reason for contempt toward any person. The list in 1:9-10 includes liars and murderers alongside sexual sins, so that no reader stands outside it, and Paul's next words call himself the worst of sinners.

It is not against marriage, food or the body. The false teachers forbade marriage and foods; Paul says that “every creation of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected” (4:4).

And it is not a call to put any ruler or party first. Paul asks the church to pray “for kings and all those in authority” (2:2), whoever they are, so that believers may live quiet and godly lives. Prayer for rulers is not the same as loyalty to a side, and the letter's one King is God: “the King of kings and Lord of lords” (6:15).

Read it as a real letter to a real person in a particular crisis. At each step, ask what problem in Ephesus Paul is facing.

Watch for the ‘trustworthy sayings’ (1:15; 3:1; 4:9), which seem to quote early Christian teaching, and for the contrast between healthy teaching and the sick speculation of the false teachers.

Notice the short songs and confessions about Christ (1:15; 2:5-6; 3:16; 6:15-16). The letter's rules are built around them.

Where the letter is debated, on women, on church leaders and on who wrote it, read the case of more than one side before you settle, and notice that Christians who share the same faith in Christ reach different conclusions. Hold your own view as one who may yet be taught.

And let the letter ask you its questions. Is your faith producing love from a pure heart? Are you content? Whom do you pray for, including those in power? And if you lead anyone, is your character the kind Paul describes?

The notes on each chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

hard.line: The list of lawbreakers, and the word the BSB renders ‘homosexuals’. Both readings, and three things that are plain on either.
‘Handed over to Satan.’ Church discipline meant to correct, and never to silence the harmed.
‘For kings and all those in authority.’ Prayer for every ruler, and no party lesson.
‘I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority.’ What all agree, and the complementarian and egalitarian readings.
‘Saved through childbearing.’ The main readings, and why no woman's worth depends on bearing children.
‘The husband of but one wife.’ Four readings of one phrase.
‘The women.’ Deacons' wives, or women deacons?
‘The Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe.’ What the verse says, and does not say.
Accusations against elders: fairness to the accused, and never a way to silence a report of abuse.
‘Use a little wine.’ Abstinence and moderation, each fairly.
Slaves and masters. Why Paul did not command the end of slavery, and the misuse of these verses.
‘The love of money is the root of all kinds of evil.’ Not money itself, and not a promise of wealth.

words.line: Greek hugiainō, to be healthy. Teaching that makes people spiritually well (1:10; 6:3).
Greek eusebeia, reverence for God lived out in daily life. More common in these letters than anywhere else in the New Testament (4:7-8; 6:6).
The inner sense that judges your own conduct. Throw away a good conscience and faith runs aground (1:19).
Paul's mark for a saying of the early church that he quotes and stands behind (1:15; 3:1; 4:9).
Greek mesitēs, a go-between who brings two sides together. ‘One mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus’ (2:5).
A price paid to set others free. Christ ‘gave Himself as a ransom for all’ (2:6).
Greek authenteō, used only here in the New Testament (2:12). Some read it as to lead or have authority; others as to domineer.
Greek episkopos, one who watches over. Later the word for bishop; in this letter a local church leader, it seems the same person as an elder (3:1).
Greek diakonos, servant. A recognized group in the church, chosen for character (3:8-13).
Greek presbuteros. Leaders of the church; those who lead well, especially in preaching and teaching, deserve ‘double honor’ (5:17).
Greek autarkeia, a word the Stoic teachers prized. For Paul, contentment rests in God, who provides (6:6-8).
The faith handed to Timothy to guard, like money left with a trusted friend (6:20).

timeline.what: Paul meets Timothy at Lystra, and Timothy joins him (Acts 16:1-3).
Paul spends about three years in Ephesus. A large church grows up (Acts 19; 20:31).
Paul says goodbye to the elders of Ephesus and warns that false teachers will rise from among them (Acts 20:17-38).
Paul under guard in Rome for two years, where Acts ends (Acts 28:30-31).

timeline.when: About AD 62 to 64, if Paul wrote it
timeline.what: Released, Paul travels again. He leaves Timothy in Ephesus, goes on to Macedonia, and writes 1 Timothy.

timeline.when: About AD 80 to 110, on another view
timeline.what: Scholars who think a follower of Paul wrote the Pastoral Letters usually date them here.
Clement of Rome writes that Paul reached ‘the limit of the west’, which many take as a sign of travels after Acts.
The Roman governor Pliny writes of questioning two slave women whom the Christians called ministers.
Irenaeus quotes 1 Timothy and names Paul as its writer.
The name ‘Pastoral Letters’ comes into use for 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus.

places.name: Ephesus
places.line: The leading city of Asia, with its great temple of Artemis. Paul left Timothy here to correct the church's own teachers (1:3).

places.name: Philippi
places.line: A city of Macedonia. Paul says he went on to Macedonia (1:3); the letter does not say where in it he was.

places.name: Thessalonica
places.line: The capital of Macedonia, where Paul had founded a church years before (Acts 17). The letter does not say whether he was here.

places.name: Lystra
places.line: Timothy's home town, where Paul met him, the son of a Jewish believing mother and a Greek father (Acts 16:1).

teaching.mapNote: Timothy stayed in Ephesus, in the province of Asia. Paul had gone on to Macedonia, across the Aegean Sea. Timothy's home was Lystra, far inland.
